reference_query_plan.central_topic: How few comparisons have to be dropped or flipped to change the top-1 or top-k set of a Bradley-Terry leaderboard. The size is measured with a one-step influence (AMIP-style) search verified by exact refits, and is compared across crowdsourced votes (Chatbot Arena 140k), expert and LLM-judge annotations (MT-Bench human and GPT-4 pairs), and sports results (NBA seasons), with synthetic and permutation controls.
comparators: Random-subset perturbation baseline (the run reports the log2 size ratio vs random)
Influence functions and leave-one-out / infinitesimal-jackknife approximations
Data-dropping robustness metrics for statistical conclusions (Broderick et al.)
Adversarial manipulation and vote rigging of pairwise rank aggregation and crowdsourced LLM leaderboards
Statistical uncertainty for Bradley-Terry rankings (bootstrap / asymptotic confidence intervals) and top-K ranking theory
core_methods: Bradley-Terry maximum-likelihood (ridge-regularized, ties as half wins) fitted to pairwise comparison data
Approximate Maximum Influence Perturbation (AMIP): first-order, influence-function ranking of rows by their effect on the leader-challenger margin
Exponential + binary prefix search with exact refits to verify the smallest perturbation set that changes the ranking
Two perturbation types (dropping rows, flipping outcomes) and two targets (top-1, top-k set)
forbidden_query_patterns: Any query copying the research question title, e.g. 'stability of pairwise comparison leaderboards' or 'sensitivity of Bradley-Terry rankings to data perturbation' (the task forbids retrieving the prior published study or pages citing it)
Queries naming 'dropping a handful of preferences' / Huang et al. follow-ups or 'who cites' style queries that could surface the forbidden paper or derivative discussions
Generic filler: 'machine learning benchmarking', 'robust optimization', 'scientific method', 'paper writing'
Chronology or search-process queries (cycle names, knapsack/relinearized variant names, harness/infra failures)
Queries for the untested category-count knapsack variant as if it were a validated contribution
Generic LLM leaderboard survey queries with no link to pairwise comparison, influence or manipulation

queries.query: approximate maximum influence perturbation dropping small fraction of data robustness
queries.rationale: The search used in every reported number is AMIP-style. This query retrieves Broderick et al. and follow-ups on exact or certified versions of the drop-data metric, and on where the first-order approximation fails, which is needed to describe our sizes as upper bounds.

queries.query: influence functions infinitesimal jackknife approximate leave-one-out generalized linear models
queries.rationale: The one-step influence score is a Newton/influence approximation for a logistic-type GLM, as in Koh & Liang. This query grounds the approximation and its accuracy, including the known gaps when many points are removed together.

queries.query: Bradley-Terry model maximum likelihood estimation existence MM algorithm paired comparisons
queries.rationale: The estimator is a ridge-regularized Bradley-Terry MLE, so we need the classic model, Zermelo/Ford existence conditions (relevant when dropped rows disconnect the graph) and Hunter's MM fitting.

queries.query: top-K ranking from pairwise comparisons sample complexity spectral MLE
queries.rationale: Our top-k-set targets and the margin dependence of fragility link to theory on when top-K sets can be identified from noisy comparisons (Rank Centrality, spectral MLE). Reviewers will expect this literature.

queries.query: adversarial manipulation of rank aggregation from pairwise comparisons
queries.rationale: Flipping or dropping comparisons to change a ranking is a data-poisoning attack on rank aggregation. This is the closest comparator literature to the flip/drop sets, alongside the starter vote-rigging paper.

queries.query: Chatbot Arena crowdsourced pairwise human preference LLM evaluation leaderboard
queries.rationale: Arena-140k is the main crowdsourced dataset. This query grounds the platform design, how its rankings are computed (BT with bootstrap CIs) and the known critiques of it.

queries.query: LLM-as-a-judge agreement with human expert pairwise judgments biases
queries.rationale: MT-Bench human vs GPT-4 judgments are our second evaluation design, and their fragility differs. Work on judge bias and on human-judge agreement explains why the two can differ.

queries.query: Elo rating predictive accuracy professional sports paired comparison
queries.rationale: The NBA seasons are the sports-design control, which has a dense, balanced schedule. This query grounds rating systems for sports results and their link to Bradley-Terry.

queries.query: confidence intervals uncertainty quantification Bradley-Terry ranking bootstrap
queries.rationale: Worst-case perturbation sizes are a different notion of uncertainty from the sampling-based bootstrap/asymptotic CIs that leaderboards publish. This query retrieves ranking-inference work so we can compare the two notions; the run computes no CIs on rankings itself.

result_driven_themes: Large crowdsourced leaderboards can be extremely fragile in relative terms: dropping about 0.05% of Arena-140k votes changes the top-1
Small expert or LLM-judge datasets need a much larger fraction to change the top-1 (about 2.7% for MT-Bench human, about 6% for MT-Bench GPT-4); sports seasons fall in between (about 0.9%)
Influence-guided sets are about 16x smaller than random subsets (mean log2 ratio about 4.0), so the gap between worst-case and average-case sensitivity is large
Fragility depends on the margin between adjacent ranks and on the comparison graph design, not only on dataset size, so a dataset-size-normalized fraction is needed for comparisons across designs
The refined search variants (category-count relinearized knapsack) were never evaluated because of infrastructure failures; the reported sizes are upper bounds from the AMIP search

Same model responses, different evaluation design: on MT-Bench, human expert and GPT-4 judges give different fragility
